reason: B is easier to learn from: it opens with a plain summary, explains Redis, Lua and the fixed window, tells you how to read the diagram, and splits the flow into labelled parts, while A is a denser list of decisions that assumes you already know the context.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it opens by explaining how the gateway works today and where the new check fits, then gives a scannable list of decisions, a separate failure-cases section and an explicit out-of-scope list. A is better at defining stack terms like Redis and Lua for a newcomer, but B makes it easier to see what the whole system does.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow for someone new: it opens with a three-phase overview, defines even basic terms (replica, lease, idempotent), explains why each design choice was made (the outbox instead of app.jobs, control rows instead of flags), and defines one reusable switch procedure, while A is denser, points ahead to steps it hasn't introduced yet, and leaves terms like advisory locks and gates for the reader to piece together.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with a three-phase overview (mirror, switch, finish), defines every term in plain language, explains the reasons behind its key choices, and uses one switch procedure for the switch, the rollback and the finish, so a newcomer can build a clear picture before reading the checklist; B is dense, and it uses undefined shorthand (`sot`, "copy lock") and refers ahead to step numbers.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with one mental model: a source of truth and a follower, where every write commits, makes a quick copy, then gets repaired, and the roles simply swap at the switch. It also explains why each design choice was made, so a newcomer understands the system before reaching the steps; A reads more like an operator's runbook of rules and procedures.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A starts with one model that works the same in both directions: source of truth and follower, then commit with outbox, quick copy, and repair. Its names for the two databases match each other, and its design decisions explain why each choice was made. A newcomer gets the whole picture before the steps begin, whereas Document B is a thorough runbook whose mechanism has to be pieced together from rules spread across the steps.

author: haiku
reason: A explains each rollback step the same way (what starts it, what it does, where its data lives, how it fails, when it moves on) and adds a full failure table without contradicting itself, while B, though easier to read at first, says a rollback "always ends in old_only" but later says "the rollout returns to shadow", which leaves a newcomer unsure how the system behaves.

author: haiku
reason: A builds a clearer mental model faster for a newcomer: a glossary, a diagram with a note that the rollback boxes are not billing_mode values, and short rule lists. B's flat diagram, step-by-step detail and 14 open questions read more like an implementation spec than an explanation of how the system works.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to learn from as an outsider: it defines even basic terms like billing period and payment provider, states the two rules that shape the design before the details, lists each reconcile outcome, and explains why charge safety cannot rely on the flag. A is tighter but assumes more context.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a full glossary and the two rules the design must keep, then explains why the way back closes at day 35 and covers infrastructure failures in a full table, so a newcomer gets the whole model faster, even though B's settle/pending-entry handling of in-flight charges is more rigorous.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to take in: it names the four endings up front, defines even basic terms (service, event, outbox), walks the flow in plain numbered steps, keeps the diagram small enough to follow and closes with a short "why the flow is safe" list, whereas A covers more edge cases (retry job, watchdog, re-reserve) but buries them in a very dense flowchart.

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term before it is used and states the four outcomes up front. Its plain-words flow matches a diagram simple enough to follow, so a newcomer can understand the whole system quickly; B covers more edge cases (retry job, watchdog, re-reservation, open-order check), but its diagram is dense and some of its terms are never defined, which makes it harder to learn the system from.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to start with because of its reading guide and red-bordered failure boxes, but A gives a newcomer a fuller and more consistent picture: every step follows the same Starts/Does/Keeps/If-it-goes-wrong layout, it explains the attemptId and inbox mechanisms, and its failure table covers cases B leaves out or treats as assumptions (Cart call failure, Inventory never answering, lost webhook, success arriving after cancellation), while B contradicts itself on cart-id versus per-attempt dedupe.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to get into: it opens with a one-sentence happy path, explains how to read the diagram, and defines the basic terms (webhook, outbox, hold vs claim, unique constraint), and its diagram boxes are short, while B covers more failure cases (Inventory never answering, a lost webhook, success arriving for a cancelled order) but in denser boxes and with less explanation of terms.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to start with: it opens with the current state (what the monolith, MailRelay and the broker are, the daily volume of each type, and why duplicates happen), defines even basic terms, and sets out a few invariants such as one owner per row that explain the whole design. A, by contrast, starts with dense schema and shadow-comparison details before the reader knows what they are for.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the current system and defines every external piece (MailRelay, the broker, flags, ack, p99, page on-call), and it gives seven numbered invariants that let a newcomer understand why the design is safe before the rollout steps start; B has a cleaner per-component runtime section, but it assumes more context and adds more moving parts (shadow hashes, reconciler, dual outboxes) without that grounding.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A covers the whole runtime model in one place before the rollout: the current worker's behaviour, the ownership rule, topics, message shapes, and every loop on both sides, and it ends with a failure table, which makes the system quicker to understand. Document B scatters the mechanics of the relay and the service across its rollout steps, even though it explains terms like SKIP LOCKED and includes a state diagram.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer more to stand on: it explains how today's system behaves (callers, the old worker's 5 s batches of 50, what counts as "accepted"), uses a simpler fixed-at-insert ownership rule, and adds a timeline table, a failure-to-outcome table and explicit open questions, so the whole system is easier to take in than A's denser state-transition design.

author: haiku
reason: Document B opens with the four open choices and how each was decided, gives a reason for every decision in its table, explains stack-specific ideas such as advisory locks, conditional UPDATE and why state must be shared across instances, and walks through a numeric example of the sliding lockout window, so a newcomer learns why the system works as it does; Document A is tighter but assumes the reader already knows the setup.

author: haiku
reason: B is tighter: it starts with the current system (two instances, no sticky sessions), shows the schema in one block, and gathers every outcome into one status/body/cookie table, while A spreads the same behavior across a long glossary, a decisions table and a rules section, and explains basics like cookies and HTTP 302 that a smart engineer already knows.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by describing the existing system (server-rendered app, two instances with no sticky sessions, the shape of the users table). It then defines its terms and goes through each step the same way: what starts it, what it does, what data it touches and what happens on failure. A newcomer can follow that more easily than B's denser prose, though B adds a few extra details.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because it first lays out the existing system (two instances, no sticky sessions, the shape of the users table) and defines its terms, then walks through each step by what starts it, what it does, what data it touches and how it fails, plus a separate failure table; A is just as rigorous but goes straight into dense decisions without that grounding.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how the app reads keys at runtime first and then gives rollout steps that run in plain order, so a newcomer can build a mental model easily; B defines more stack terms, but its steps run out of numeric order (16 and 17 before 12, 15 before 14) and it is much longer, which makes it harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: B explains how the app reads keys at runtime before the rollout, lists its steps in the order they run, and puts access and failure/rollback in tables, while A has a longer glossary but its numbered steps need two out-of-order exceptions (16-17 before 12, 15 before 14) and it leaves the runtime model until the end, so the whole system is harder to follow.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains more of what a newcomer is missing: it describes the current system in more detail (keys read at import, module-level client singletons, a /healthz that returns 200 as soon as the server listens), defines stack terms that A takes for granted (pod, readiness probe, canary, SecretProvider), and gives a one-line overview of the step order plus a failure summary table, so the whole system is easier to grasp, even though B is longer.

author: sonnet
reason: For an outsider, Document A is easier to follow: it defines the infrastructure terms (pod, readiness probe, canary), explains the current behaviour and the two-part structure up front, and ends with a failure-summary table, while B is tighter but assumes more prior context.

author: haiku
reason: A has a component diagram of the whole system and walks through every flow with the exact queries, lock points and responses, so its picture is complete and consistent; B defines more basic terms, but its diagrams hide the transaction details and its step numbering contradicts itself (for example, "steps 4 to 9" against "steps 6 to 8" for the same transaction).

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a summary and a component diagram that maps the whole system, then walks each flow with concrete SQL-level steps, a failure table and explicit open questions, and it stays consistent throughout; A explains its terms more gently, but it contradicts itself on what the worker does after a failed send (drop silently in one place, invalidate the link and alert in another) and its step numbering does not match its labels.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a system map, defines "token check" once and reuses it, splits the flow into numbered steps with GET and POST kept apart, and explains why each choice was made (mail scanners following GET links, the referrer leak, the crash between separate writes), which makes it easier for a newcomer to follow than A's crowded, misaligned branch diagram.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a clear diagram of the whole system and defines "token check" once for reuse. Its three flows are numbered steps that stay internally consistent: the reply goes out before the lookup, and it explains why GET must not use up the link. B has a friendlier prose summary, but its request diagram is a cluttered tangle of misaligned branches, and its "off the response path where possible" contradicts the flow it draws.
